messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan is a 32-year-old park ranger who had spent years feeling most at ease in remote places, but that changed after he was captured and tortured while working alone in a backcountry area. He can only tell the beginning and end in any coherent way. He remembers with terrible sharpness the scrape of a door, the sound of a lock, the sensation of being pinned and the conviction that his body was being damaged in some permanent way. Other stretches are missing entirely. When he tries to explain what happened, he loses the thread, stops mid-sentence, and says the whole thing exists more as bursts in his body than as a story he can tell. Those jagged, nonverbal fragments have come to mean something alarming to him: if the memory is this broken and if his reactions still feel so overwhelming, he has started to fear he is going crazy.

In the months afterward, Ethan came to believe that what happened had left him physically vulnerable and fundamentally unable to rely on anyone else to keep him safe. That belief has shaped how he moves through daily life. Living alone, he checks doors and windows repeatedly at night, not once but again and again until he is briefly satisfied. He rehearses what he will say before almost any interaction, including routine exchanges with visitors at the park station, as though being unprepared with other people could expose him. He also avoids driving or even riding in a vehicle when he can, because he no longer trusts his body or other people enough to tolerate the feeling of being confined and dependent. The more he lives this way, cut off behind preparation and control, the more convinced he becomes that he really cannot rely on others and that something in him has been permanently altered.

His memory difficulties intensify this pattern. Certain moments of the torture are extremely clear while others are blank, and the mismatch torments him. A delayed radio response, a truck that does not arrive when expected, or a colleague who is late meeting him on a trail can pull him instantly back into those isolated fragments without warning. His body reacts before his mind has caught up; his chest tightens, his muscles brace, and he is already scanning for danger before he can tell himself where he is. Because the memory comes in flashes he cannot fully explain, he tries to manage it by numbing his feelings and by overpreparing for contact with other people. He says less, feels less, and scripts conversations in advance so he will not be thrown off by questions he cannot answer. Yet this very narrowing seems to leave the memory even less speakable, more like raw sensation than narrative.

At work, the problem is especially visible. As a ranger, he is expected to drive between sites, check trailheads, and respond flexibly when conditions change. Ethan now rearranges tasks to avoid getting into a vehicle whenever possible and grows visibly tense when a patrol return is delayed. If another ranger is ten minutes late, he is immediately certain something bad is happening. In those moments he starts checking locks at the station or the cabin compulsively, as if securing the perimeter might get ahead of whatever threat is already underway. The body-first alarm he experiences makes the world feel dangerous in a constant, preconscious way, and from there it is a short step to the thought that his nervous system has been damaged beyond repair. Each surge of threat seems to confirm his belief that he is physically vulnerable and losing his mind.

That same alarm also disturbs the memory itself. When he gets activated by a delay or a noise around a door, the clearest pieces of the torture rush forward while the rest disappears. He becomes less able to put words to what happened and more certain that there is something terribly wrong with him because he cannot produce a full account. To prevent that disorganization, he rehearses interactions in advance and keeps himself emotionally flat, but afterward he often notices that he remembers even less of what he wanted to say. He leaves conversations ashamed and unsettled, taking his own numbing and avoidance as further proof that he has changed for the worse.

By the time he sought help, Ethan’s world had narrowed around these efforts to stay ahead of danger. His work performance had begun to suffer because he was dodging drives, overchecking doors, and struggling whenever plans shifted. He is coming to treatment not because he feels safe enough to talk, but because he is frightened by how quickly his body reacts, how impossible the memory is to tell, and how certain he has become that if this continues he will end up completely alone, trapped with a mind and body he can no longer trust.
